title: Toronto Police shootings inquest hears Sylvia Klibingaitis bone-chilling 911 call
article: It's a bone-chilling call for help from an eerily calm woman gripped in the vice of psychotic delusions, a woman convinced she was "pure evil."
"I'm about to kill people," Sylvia Klibingaitis tells the 911 operator in a flat voice. "I have a deadly weapon and I intend to use it."
But there would be no help in time for Klibingaitis. Minutes later, she would be dead from a police bullet.

At the coroner's inquest looking into the Toronto Police shootings of Klibingaitis and two others with mental illness, her psychiatrist described a troubled 52-year-old grandmother consumed by religious delusions that she was damned by God and destined to live out her life poor and homeless.

In 2009, she was hospitalized at CAMH and prescribed an anti-psychotic drug. But after almost two years on the strong medication, she told Dr. Jorge Soni that she stopped taking it. She didn't like the side effects and didn't feel it was working.

When the psychiatrist saw her over the summer of 2011, she had lost her job and was worried she'd soon be homeless because her elderly mother, with whom she lived, might soon have to move into a nursing home. There was also the added stress of her 18-year-old daughter and grandson moving to Chile.

Soni said he originally believed she was suffering from a bipolar disorder with psychotic features and then changed his diagnosis to obsessive compulsive disorder with psychotic features. Her religious delusions of eternal damnation never abated.

On Sept. 27, 2011, Klibingaitis was in crisis. Agitated, worried about her daughter and convinced she was going to be punished by God for past sins, she told her psychiatrist that she needed to check herself back into CAMH. With his office just next door, he walked her over to the emergency department and then left to complete the paperwork she would need for the voluntary admission.
But when he returned to the hospital, Klibingaitis was gone.

Soni said he called her immediately to find out why she had left. In a much calmer voice, she told him that she was feeling better and was going to have dinner with her daughter instead. Because she didn't pose a threat to herself or others, he explained, no one could commit her to the hospital against her will. They made an appointment for a month later.
She would never make it.
Ten days later, Klibingaitis made her fateful call to 911.

In the nine-minute tape played for the inquest jury Wednesday, Klibingaitis can be heard speaking in a monotone as the operator deftly manages to get as much information as she can. In that frighteningly flat tone, she says she's holding a foot-long knife in her mom's bedroom while the elderly woman is in the bathroom, unaware her daughter is contemplating murder.
"Ma'am, why do you want to kill your mother?" she's asked.
"I'm pure evil," she says simply.
Klibingaitis is asked to leave the bedroom and put down the knife.
"I'm holding it," she replies.
"Can you please put it down?"
"No," says Klibingaitis.
The astute operator has quickly surmised what is happening. "Have you been diagnosed with psychiatric problems?" she asks gently.
"Yes," replies Klibingaitis. "Bipolar."
Yet sadly, her psychiatrist isn't contacted nor is anyone else with mental health experience. Would that have stopped this inevitable tragedy?

Buying time, with police on the way, the 911 operator asks what happened that morning to make her pick up the knife. Klibingaitis doesn't answer. She asks her again to leave the bedroom. She says she can't, the phone isn't portable.

And then Klibingaitis doesn't speak again. Instead, all that can be heard from inside the home is the voice of her Lithuanian mother who must have been noticing the police arriving outside: "Something very bad happen in our neighbourhood," she says.
She was horribly right. Her daughter had put down the phone and according to an SIU investigation that cleared the officer, she came out and rushed directly toward the police with her knife raised.
He fired three bullets. By the time paramedics arrived at 9:46 a.m., officers were desperately performing CPR, but it was too late. Klibingaitis died of a gunshot wound to the chest.
That poor sick woman was certain she was doomed. And so she was.
